Here, using the Community Earth System Model (CESM2) under different CO 2 emission rates, we find a pronounced weakening of ocean CO 2 uptake in the Subpolar North Atlantic (SPNA), distinct from the global response.
Initially, the SPNA is an effective CO 2 sink, but due to the contraction of deep convection, the uptake decreases and the oceanic pCO 2 exceeds the global average.

Recognizing the importance of regional ocean circulation in CO 2 uptake, we identify a nonlinear relationship between environmental conditions and uptake response, revealing consistent thresholds for the emergence of uptake weakening.
These findings are also reproduced in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6, confirming their robustness.

Methods CO 2 emission rate (ER) experiments design The Community Earth System Model, version 2 (CESM2) was used to conduct an idealized CO 2 emission-driven simulation in this study.

The components of the model, including the Community Atmospheric Model, Version 6 (CAM6) for the atmosphere, and the Community Land Model Version 5 (CLM5) for the land 60 , are implemented with a spatial resolution of approximately ~1° and 32 vertical levels.
The ocean carbon cycles in CESM2 are depicted by the Marine Biogeochemistry Library (MARBL) 63 .
We designed a series of idealized simulations with different CO 2 emission rate (ER) to explore the pathway dependency (Fig.
We first conducted an experiment in which anthropogenic CO 2 emissions increase linearly to 30 PgC yr –1 from 2001 to 2100, based on the business-as-usual scenario (SSP5-8.5), referred to ER1.0.
We further integrated ER1.5, in which anthropogenic CO 2 emissions increase linearly to 45 PgC yr –1 from 2001 to 2100, which is 1.5 times the emission rate of ER1.0.
Note that ER0.5 is integrated into 2150 (an additional 50 years) to simulate substantial global warming.

These experiments are driven by the emission, which means that the atmospheric CO 2 concentration is determined not only by prescribed anthropogenic CO 2 emissions but also by oceanic and terrestrial CO 2 fluxes interactively, thereby reflecting changes in CO 2 concentration via the carbon cycle-climate feedback.
